kurals.tamil:
சிறுமை நமக்கொழியச் சேட்சென்றார் உள்ளி
நறுமலர் நாணின கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirumai namakkozhiyach chaetchendraar ulli
narumalar naanina kan.
kurals.meaning: Thinking of the one who went far away and left this sorrow behind with us, your eyes have wept away their beauty, so that now they are ashamed to face the fragrant flowers they once outshone.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a girl whose eyes were once as bright as the flowers in her garden. Her dearest person goes on a long trip, and she cries so much that her eyes become red and tired. Now when she looks at the fresh flowers, she feels shy, because the flowers look brighter than her eyes do.
kurals.university: Chapter 124, uṟuppu nalaṉ aḻital (‘the wasting of the beauty of the limbs’), continues the kaṟpiyal sequence on separation (pirivu): the wife, parted from her husband, loses her nalam (bodily loveliness) limb by limb, eyes, shoulders, bangles, forehead. Pope’s prose gloss (‘your eyes weep for him who is gone afar’) follows the traditional reading, associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the confidante (tōḻi) speaks to the heroine. The key words are ciṟumai (here ‘distress, grief’, glossed துன்பம் by Mu. Varadarasanar), cēṭ ceṉṟār (‘he who has gone far’), and naṟumalar nāṇiṉa kaṇ (‘the eyes were ashamed before fragrant flowers’): Sangam convention compares a woman’s eyes to blue water-lilies (kuvaḷai), so eyes that once shamed the flowers now hang back before them. Solomon Pappaiah reads ciṟumai as the ‘weakness of not bearing separation’ left with her while he bore it and went. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word (உறுப்புநலனழிதல்), thirukkural.net as two (உறுப்புநலன் அழிதல்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman finally finds Sita in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, she is thin from fasting and grief, her face wet with tears, sighing again and again, a woman whose beauty is dimmed like a moon behind cloud as she thinks only of the far-off Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows separation from the beloved literally wearing away the heroine’s radiance.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita’s eyes and looks are spent by weeping for a husband who is far away.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the wasting-by-grief motif fits closely, though Sita is a captive rather than a wife left at home, and there is no flower comparison.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members are as a shadow.”
christianity.explanation: Job describes grief so heavy that it dims his eyes and leaves his whole body a shadow of itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes the eye the first part of the body to lose its brightness under sorrow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); strong match on grief dimming the eyes, though Job’s sorrow is not for an absent lover.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells how Jacob’s long grief for his lost son Joseph physically ruined his eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, longing for one who is far away is written on the eyes, which lose their former lustre.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); close physical parallel, though the longing is a father’s for his son, not a wife’s for her husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eye is dimmed because of vexation; It waxeth old because of all mine adversaries.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist, worn out with weeping through the night, says his eye has aged and dimmed from distress.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise ‘grow old’ before their time, losing the beauty that once outshone the flowers.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917; verse 6:7 in Christian numbering); good match on eyes wasted by sorrow, though the cause is enemies, not separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the story told when the Buddha first visited Rahula’s mother (Yasodhara), King Suddhodana relates that after the prince left home she lived as he did: on hearing he wore yellow robes she wore yellow, she ate one meal a day as he did, and she gave up garlands and perfumes.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka commentary portrays the deserted wife setting aside flowers and adornment out of loyalty to her absent husband.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns away from fragrant flowers, her beauty given up to grief for the one who went far away.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka 485), introductory story (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a commentarial frame story, not verified against a live text this session; the renounced flowers fit, but Yasodhara’s austerity is a chosen discipline rather than involuntary wasting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: When Arishtanemi (Neminatha) left his own wedding procession to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati lost all her joy.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s brightness, like the heroine’s eyes in the Kural, is extinguished at once by the departure of the one she was to marry.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on grief at the beloved’s going, though Jain tradition turns her grief toward renunciation and the text says nothing of her eyes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Clytie, abandoned by the Sun-god she loved, sits on the bare ground for nine days without food, living only on dew and her own tears, gazing at him as he crosses the sky, until her wasted body turns into a flower that still follows the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid turns a woman’s wasting for an absent lover into a metamorphosis: her body becomes a flower.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine weeps until her eyes are outdone by flowers; Clytie weeps until she becomes one.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; tears, wasting and flowers all match, though the Sun has rejected Clytie rather than merely travelled away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover’s soul when parted from the beautiful one: the openings through which its wings grew dry up and close, and the soul, stung all over, writhes in pain, until the sight of the beloved again refreshes it.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats separation from the beloved as a bodily-feeling drought that withers the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows the same drying and withering, but on the outside, in eyes that lose their bloom.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; a real account of the pain of separation, though Plato’s withering is of the soul’s wings rather than the eyes.

kurals.tamil:
நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்
பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayandhavar nalkaamai solluva poalum
pasandhu panivaarum kan.
kurals.meaning: My eyes, gone sallow and streaming with tears, seem to tell everyone that the one I love has stopped showing me his kindness.
kurals.elementary: When you are sad, you might try to hide it, but your red, teary eyes give you away, and people can guess something is wrong. The girl in this verse feels her pale, wet eyes are telling the whole town that the person she loves is far away and not caring for her right now.
kurals.university: The heroine imagines her eyes as informers: pasantu (‘having turned sallow’, from pacappu/pacalai, the greenish-yellow pallor of love-sickness that Chapter 119 treats at length) and paṉi vārum (‘streaming with dew’, i.e. tears) they ‘seem to speak’ (colluva pōlum) of nayantavar nalkāmai, the ‘unkindness’ or ‘failure to bestow grace’ of the one she desired. Nalkāmai is the negative of nalku, ‘to show favour, to be gracious’, a word used of kings and gods as well as lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that the eyes tell this ‘to others’ (piṟarkku), which makes the poem about exposure as much as grief: the body betrays what modesty (nāṇ) would conceal. Pope renders: ‘The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears, / As witness of the lover’s lack of love appears.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend goes to Krishna and describes Radha’s state in his absence: she finds sandal paste and moonlight painful, she is wasted and tearful, and her whole condition testifies to his neglect.
hinduism.explanation: The friend’s report makes Radha’s suffering body the evidence of Krishna’s absence.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Kural the heroine’s pale, tearful eyes play the friend’s part, announcing the lover’s unkindness to everyone.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the canto’s substance, not verified line by line; strong fit on bodily signs reporting a lover’s neglect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist points to his worn-out eye as visible proof of his distress.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise display inner grief openly, as if testifying to it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); good on eyes consumed by grief, but there is no beloved whose unkindness is being revealed.

islam.quote_or_event: In The Ring of the Dove, Ibn Hazm lists the outward signs by which love betrays itself, such as the lover’s fixed gaze, sleeplessness, sighing, and, when the beloved is absent or unkind, wasting and pallor that others can read.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar treats the lover’s body as a text that onlookers can read even when the lover keeps silent.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears exactly this: her pale, wet eyes are telling others what she would not say.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on the signs of love (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of Arberry’s translation, not verified this session; the signs-of-love catalogue fits well, though it is a treatise on love, not scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes do fail with tears, mine inwards burn, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the breach of the daughter of my people.”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations describes eyes exhausted by tears as the outward face of a heartbreak.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s tear-streaming eyes are likewise the visible sign of an inner wound.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; matches tear-worn eyes, but the grief is national catastrophe, not a lover’s neglect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha asks which is greater, the water of the four oceans or the tears his monks have shed over the long round of births while weeping at union with what is displeasing and separation from what is pleasing; the tears, he says, are greater.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta makes separation from the dear the source of an ocean of tears.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s streaming eyes are one small instance of the tears the Buddha says separation always brings.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; good on tears of separation, though the Buddhist point is to end attachment, not to reproach a lover.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana’s lecture on carelessness teaches that the eye’s attachment to pleasing colour and form leads to suffering: one who is passionately fond of colours comes to grief and is never satisfied.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces the misery of the senses to raga, attachment, beginning with the eye.
jainism.tie_back: In the Kural the eye that once delighted in the beloved is now the very organ that suffers and shows the loss, which Jain doctrine would read as the fruit of attachment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32, verses on the eye and colour (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; the Jain text condemns sensory attachment rather than sympathising with a lover, so it reframes the Kural instead of echoing it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Penelope listens to the disguised Odysseus tell of her husband, her tears flow down her cheeks like snow melting on the mountain-tops, so that her fair cheeks seem to dissolve as she weeps for the man who is sitting beside her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures a faithful wife’s face visibly wasting with tears for a long-absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s melting cheeks, like the Kural’s streaming eyes, publish her grief for an absent husband before others.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.204-209 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile; strong match on tears showing an absent husband’s cost, though Penelope does not accuse Odysseus of unkindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how the physician Erasistratus discovered that Prince Antiochus was wasting away from a hidden love for his stepmother Stratonice: whenever she entered, the prince showed Sappho’s symptoms, faltering speech, burning flushes, pallor and sudden faintness.
philosophy.explanation: A Greek physician reads a secret love straight off a patient’s body.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears the same thing: her pallid, wet eyes tell onlookers what she has not said.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius 38 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Bernadotte Perrin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested anecdote; excellent fit on the body betraying love, though here the lover is a man and the love unrequited for a different reason.

kurals.tamil:
தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்
மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thanandhamai saala arivippa poalum
manandha-naal veengiya thoal.
kurals.meaning: My shoulders, which swelled with joy on the day we were joined, have grown thin, and now they seem to announce our separation loudly to all.
kurals.elementary: Think of a balloon at a birthday party, round and full, and then the same balloon a week later, small and wrinkled. The girl’s arms were full and strong when she was happy with the person she loves; now that he is away they have become thin, and anyone can see that she misses him.
kurals.university: The contrast is temporal and physical: maṇanta nāḷ (‘the day of union’, which may mean the wedding day or any day of togetherness) set against taṇantamai (‘the having-parted’, from taṇa, ‘to separate’). Vīṅkiya tōḷ (‘shoulders that swelled’) uses the Sangam convention that a woman’s tōḷ, shoulders or upper arms, grow plump (pūrittal) in happiness and thin in grief, so they become public evidence; cāla aṟivippa pōlum means ‘they seem to proclaim it fully’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all add that the thinning announces the separation ‘to others’, continuing the motif of 1232 in which the body exposes private grief. Pope: ‘These withered arms, desertion’s pangs abundantly display, / That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day.’ Pope transliterates the compound as ‘manandha-naal’; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the Tamil text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Nala story, Damayanti, longing for Nala after the swan’s message, grows pale and thin and loses interest in everything, until her companions report to King Bhima that his daughter is unwell, and he resolves to hold her svayamvara.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata shows a young woman’s love-sick wasting being noticed by others and reported to her father.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved’s absence is announced to the world by a body visibly growing thin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good on wasting that others notice, though Damayanti pines before marriage, not after a wedding.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By reason of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my skin.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist’s sorrow has wasted him until his body shows nothing but skin and bone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s shoulders, once full, similarly shrink and make grief visible.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); strong on bodily wasting from grief, but without a lover or the ‘then and now’ contrast.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn him that his unending remembrance of Joseph is wasting him away.
islam.tie_back: Like Jacob, the Kural’s heroine is being worn down by constant remembrance of the absent one, and onlookers can see it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); good on wasting from remembrance that others notice, though not a marital separation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her princes were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk… Their visage is blacker than coal; they are not known in the streets; their skin is shrivelled upon their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations sets the former radiance of Jerusalem’s nobles against their present shrunken, unrecognisable bodies.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same ‘then and now’ contrast between shoulders that swelled on the day of union and shoulders now wasted.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (with ellipsis); precise on the contrast of former fullness and present wasting, though the cause is famine, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that even splendid royal chariots wear out, and the body too grows old, while only the Dhamma of the good does not decay.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching treats the fading of bodily beauty as an instance of universal impermanence (anicca).
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s shoulders, full on the day of union and thin today, show that same impermanence, hastened by grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; it shares the theme of the body’s decline but speaks of age, not love-sickness.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemachandra’s account of the emperor Sanatkumara, gods come to see his famed beauty; when he proudly receives them again in royal dress, they tell him that disease has already entered his body and his beauty has faded, and he renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story makes the sudden loss of bodily beauty a lesson in the impermanence of the body.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, contrasts a body glowing on one day with the same body visibly diminished later.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 4, life of Sanatkumara (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not verified against Johnson’s text this session; it shares the fading-beauty motif but has nothing to do with love or separation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in the woods; her love clings to her and grows with grief, her body wastes with wakeful care, her skin shrivels, her moisture dries into the air, until only her voice and bones remain, and the bones turn to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a lover literally wasting away from unreturned love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s shrunken shoulders are an early stage of what Ovid carries to its end in Echo.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; precise on wasting from love, though Echo was never united with Narcissus, so the ‘day of union’ contrast is missing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that lovers waste their strength and are worn out by their labour, their life spent at another’s beck, their wealth slipping away and their good name sickening.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet counts physical wasting among the costs of romantic passion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural records the same toll on the body, though it treats the heroine with sympathy rather than as a warning.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1121-1124 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches love’s wearing effect on the body, but Lucretius is critical of passion, the Kural tender toward it.

kurals.tamil:
பணைநீங்கிப் பைந்தொடி சோரும் துணைநீங்கித்
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Panai-neengip paindhoti soarum thunaineengith
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
kurals.meaning: With your partner gone, your shoulders have lost their old beauty and their fullness, and the bright gold bangles now slip loose from your wasted arms.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever worn a ring or bracelet that fit perfectly, and then it got loose after you were sick for a while? In this verse, a girl is so sad that her loved one has gone away that she grows thin, and her bangles keep sliding off her arms.
kurals.university: The couplet builds a double loss with two parallel absolutives: paṇai nīṅki (‘the plumpness having gone’) and tuṇai nīṅki (‘the companion having gone’), so the departure of the tuṇai, the spouse, causes the departure of the paṇai, the fullness of the arm. Tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ means ‘shoulders whose former (tol) beauty (kaviṉ) has withered’, and pain̮toṭi cōrum, ‘the fresh-gold bangles slip down’, introduces the image of the loose bangle (toṭi, vaḷai) that dominates 1234-1236. The slipping bangle is a stock sign of separation in Sangam akam poetry and in Sanskrit kāvya alike. Pope’s gloss (‘In the absence of your consort, your shoulders… your bracelets… have become loose’) makes the confidante the speaker. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the shoulders as causing the bangles to slip; Kalaignar glosses paintoṭi as பசும்பொன் வளையல்கள். Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the very opening of the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, separated from his wife, has grown so thin that the golden bracelet has slipped from his forearm, leaving the wrist bare.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa uses the slipped bracelet as the first, defining image of a lover wasted by separation.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s loose bangles are exactly this sign, here worn by the abandoned wife rather than the exiled husband.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta, Purvamegha 2 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse (kanaka-valaya-bhramśa-rikta-prakoṣṭhaḥ); near one-to-one image, though worn by the man in Kalidasa.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah uses a bride’s ornaments as the image of what a loving partner would never forget.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has lost the bloom her ornaments once graced because the partner seems to have forgotten her.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares bride, ornaments and forgetting, but the forgetter is the people and the forgotten is God, the reverse of the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Layla, married against her will and separated from Majnun, pines in secret; her beauty wanes, she grows thin and pale, and she finally sickens and dies of her longing.
islam.explanation: The Persian poem makes the beloved’s slow physical wasting the measure of her hidden love.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Layla loses her former beauty because the one she loves is out of reach.
islam.source: Nizami Ganjavi, Layla and Majnun (paraphrase; cf. tr. R. Gelpke)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the story’s outline; good on wasting from separation, but it is Persian literature from a Muslim milieu, not Islamic scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And gone is from the daughter of Zion all her splendour.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations personifies Jerusalem as a woman whose former glory has departed with her losses.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, has seen her ‘old beauty’ (tolkaviṉ) depart along with her companion.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; the lost-splendour image fits, but the woman is a personified city and the loss is exile, not a husband’s absence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like rounded door-bars — both of them — my arms were once splendid. With age, they’re like dried up patali trees.” Ambapali adds that her hands, once adorned with gold and delicate rings, are now like onions and tubers.
buddhism.explanation: The former courtesan, now a nun, describes how her once-lovely arms and jewelled hands have withered.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same withering of arms that once filled their ornaments, though grief, not age, has done it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; very close on withered arms and ornaments, but the cause is ageing and the lesson impermanence, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Jain didactic anthology Naladiyar repeatedly warns that youth and bodily beauty wither like a flower, so that the body once admired soon becomes something no one wishes to look at.
jainism.explanation: Tamil Jain ethics uses the fading of beauty to turn the mind from the body to dharma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows that fading happening in a single season of grief; the Jain poets would draw from it a lesson about the body’s impermanence.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, chapters on the instability of youth and the body (paraphrase; cf. tr. G.U. Pope, 1893)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Tamil Jain work’s general teaching, without a verified verse number; shares fading beauty but none of the Kural’s sympathy for love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Writing to her husband Protesilaus at Troy, Laodamia says that while he is at war she will not dress her hair or wear gold and fine robes; she lives like a widow in mourning until he comes home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s heroine sets aside her ornaments as a sign of her husband’s absence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine does not remove her bangles; grief makes them fall away on their own.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close on ornaments and a husband away at war, but Laodamia removes them by choice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Robert Burton lists the symptoms of love-melancholy: lovers grow lean, pale and hollow-eyed, lose their appetite and sleep, and pine away, so that the disease can be read in their bodies.
philosophy.explanation: Burton’s encyclopedia of melancholy treats love-sickness as a real wasting illness with visible signs.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s thin shoulders and loose bangles are just such symptoms, recorded from the patient’s side.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2, Member 3 (Symptoms of Love-Melancholy) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of Burton; strong on visible wasting, though Burton is a learned compiler, not a philosopher of love.

kurals.tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும் தொடியொடு
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumai uraikkum thotiyodu
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
kurals.meaning: My shoulders, their old beauty faded and their bangles slipping off, proclaim to everyone the cruelty of the hard-hearted one who left me.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes our bodies tell a story we don’t say out loud, like a droopy face when we’re upset. Here the girl’s thin arms and falling bangles seem to tell the whole town, “Look how much he has hurt her by staying away so long.”
kurals.university: Koṭiyār koṭumai uraikkum (‘they speak the cruelty of the cruel one’) is an emphatic figura etymologica: koṭiyār (‘the cruel/crooked one’, honorific plural used of the husband) and koṭumai (‘cruelty’) share the root koṭu, ‘bent, harsh’. The second line repeats 1234’s tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ verbatim, a deliberate echo, while toṭiyoṭu (‘together with the bangles’) makes the slipping bracelets co-witnesses. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses koṭiyār as ‘the cruel one who does not feel my suffering’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the shoulders say it ‘for the town to know’ (ūraṟiya). The accusation is ventured here only to be withdrawn in 1236, where the heroine is pained to hear him so called. Pope: ‘These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone, / The cruelty declare of that most cruel one.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna finally comes to Radha at dawn bearing the marks of a night spent with another, she sends him away in reproach, calling him faithless and telling him to go back to the one he chose.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva gives the wronged heroine a sharp, public voice of reproach against her lover.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lets her wasted shoulders make the same charge of cruelty on her behalf.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the canto’s substance; good on a heroine accusing her lover, though Krishna’s offence is infidelity, not distance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother’s children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song explains her changed looks as the visible result of others’ harshness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise points to her altered body as proof of the harsh treatment she has suffered.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); good on a woman’s changed appearance caused by others’ harshness, though the blamed parties are her brothers, not her lover.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names a husband’s neglect or turning away as a real wrong to a wife and urges reconciliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers exactly such ‘evasion’, and her body bears witness to it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); addresses a husband’s neglect, but as law and counsel rather than as a wife’s lament.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD hath called thee as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit; and a wife of youth, can she be rejected? saith thy God.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah uses the figure of a young wife left grieving to describe Israel, and protests that such a wife cannot rightly be cast off.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is just such a ‘wife forsaken and grieved in spirit’, whose body cries out against the one who left.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; strong image of a forsaken young wife, though in Isaiah it is a metaphor for God and Israel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists a husband’s duties to his wife: to honour her, not to disparage her, to be faithful, to give her authority in the home and to provide her with adornments.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics treats a husband’s neglect of his wife as a failure of duty.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s bare, wasted arms indict a husband who has not fulfilled these duties, including the gift of ornaments that now fall away.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; it supplies the norm the absent husband falls short of, but contains no lament or accusation.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Prince Pavananjaya, offended on his wedding day, refuses even to look at his bride Anjana and neglects her for many years; she wastes away in grief, while those around her see the injustice of her lot.
jainism.explanation: The story is the Jain tradition’s classic portrait of a faithful wife wasting under a husband’s cruelty.
jainism.tie_back: Anjana’s wasted body makes the same silent accusation as the Kural’s shoulders and slipping bangles.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not verified against Johnson’s text this session; strong fit on a neglected wife’s wasting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Catullus’ telling, Ariadne, waking on Naxos to see Theseus’ ship sailing away, calls him faithless and forgetful, and cries out against the cruelty of the man for whom she gave up her home.
greek_mythology.explanation: The deserted Ariadne is the Roman poets’ model of a woman denouncing a cruel lover.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also names her lover ‘the cruel one’ (koṭiyār), though she lets her body speak the charge.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on accusing a cruel lover, though Theseus has abandoned Ariadne for good, unlike the Kural’s absent husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Pausanias says the common, bodily lover is not constant, because he loves what is itself inconstant; when the bloom of youth he desired has faded, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his promises.
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias explains a lover’s desertion as the natural result of loving only the body’s bloom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears this cruelty, her bloom gone, her lover away; Pausanias offers the philosophical diagnosis of such a lover.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; illuminates inconstant love, but reverses the Kural’s order, since there the bloom fades because the lover left.

kurals.tamil:
தொடியொடு தோள்நெகிழ நோவல் அவரைக்
கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thotiyodu thoalnekizha noval avaraik
kotiyar enakkooral nondhu.
kurals.meaning: Because my bangles slip and my shoulders have grown thin, people call him cruel; it hurts me more to hear him blamed than to bear the wasting itself.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best friend moves away for a while, and you are sad. If someone says, “Your friend is mean for leaving you,” you might feel even worse, because you still love your friend and don’t want anyone to speak badly of them. That is how the girl in this verse feels.
kurals.university: Here the tone turns: after 1235’s accusation, the heroine is pained (nōval, ‘I grieve’) when others, or the confidante, call him koṭiyar (‘cruel’) because of her loosened bangles and thinned shoulders (toṭiyoṭu tōḷ nekiḻa). The final word nontu (‘in sorrow, being hurt’) can be taken with the speakers or with the heroine, and the commentators divide: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar have the onlookers (kāṇpavar) say it, while Solomon Pappaiah makes the shoulders and bangles themselves the speakers. Pope’s gloss (‘I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man’) addresses the confidante, which accords with the reading associated with Parimelazhagar that the heroine answers her tōḻi. The ethic is the wife’s loyalty (kaṟpu), which forbids hearing the husband reproached even when she is the one who suffers. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama, bowing to public gossip, has Sita left in the forest, she sends him a message through Lakshmana that blames no one but her own fate, asks him to care for his people as he would his brothers, and says she grieves less for herself than for the slander against his name.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki’s Sita refuses to accuse the husband who has caused her suffering and worries instead about his reputation.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita is pained by his blame rather than by her own wasting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not verified line by line; strong on refusing to blame the husband, though Rama’s act is a real banishment, not an absence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul’s portrait of love describes a charity that keeps trusting and enduring instead of accusing.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows that love: she bears the wasting but will not hear her husband condemned.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); good on love that bears and believes the best, though it is a general ideal rather than a lover’s words.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that a believing man should not hate a believing woman: if he dislikes one of her traits, he will be pleased with another.
islam.explanation: The hadith asks a spouse not to define the other by a single fault.
islam.tie_back: The heroine applies this generosity in reverse: she will not let her husband be judged by the one hurt his absence causes.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge (sunnah.com did not return the page this session); a real teaching on charitable judgment of a spouse, but addressed to husbands.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah asks that others, especially companions, be judged favourably rather than condemned.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine judges her absent husband exactly so, refusing the verdict ‘cruel’ that others pass on him.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong ethical parallel for refusing to condemn a companion, though not about marriage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that the faults of others are easily seen while one’s own are hard to see, and that people winnow others’ faults like chaff.
buddhism.explanation: The verse warns against the quick, public fault-finding that comes so easily to onlookers.
buddhism.tie_back: The onlookers in the Kural do just this, pronouncing the husband cruel, and the heroine is hurt by their easy verdict.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; it criticises fault-finding in general, not the specific loyalty of a wife.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Abandoned at her wedding when Arishtanemi renounced the world, Rajimati blames her own life, not him, and resolves to follow him into the ascetic path.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati suffers the loss but will not call the one who left her cruel.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; good on not blaming the departed beloved, though her answer is renunciation rather than waiting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s shade praises Penelope above all wives because she kept faith with her absent husband through twenty years, so that the gods would make her fame a song for all mankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer holds up Penelope as the model of a wife who stays loyal to a husband who has been away for a very long time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same steadfast loyalty, defending a husband whom others are ready to condemn.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 24.192-198 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on a wife’s loyalty to an absent husband, but there is no scene of others blaming Odysseus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero says a true friend must not only refrain from bringing charges against his friend but must not even believe charges that others bring.
philosophy.explanation: On Friendship makes loyalty against outside accusation a mark of genuine love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine practises this loyalty, refusing to accept the charge of cruelty that others make against her husband.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a close ethical parallel, though Cicero speaks of friendship between men rather than marriage.

kurals.tamil:
பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே கொடியார்க்கென்
வாடுதோட் பூசல் உரைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Paadu perudhiyo nenje kotiyaarkken
vaatudhot poosal uraiththu.
kurals.meaning: O my heart, will you not win some glory by going to that hard-hearted one and telling him how loudly my wasting shoulders cry out?
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone, we talk to ourselves, like “Come on, brave heart, go tell them how we feel!” The girl in this verse talks to her own heart and asks it to go to the person she loves and tell him how sad and thin she has become.
kurals.university: The heroine now addresses her own nenjam (heart, mind) as a possible messenger, a device developed at length in the next chapter, 125 (neñcoṭu kiḷattal, ‘speaking to the heart’). Pāṭu peṟutiyō means ‘will you gain greatness/glory?’; the question can be read as an exhortation (Kalaignar: ‘will you not gain glory?’) or as a rueful challenge (Solomon Pappaiah: ‘will you gain glory by telling him these empty rumours?’). Vāṭu tōḷ pūcal is ‘the clamour of my withering shoulders’, pūcal being a noisy outcry or public uproar, so the wasting body is imagined as shouting. Koṭiyārkku (‘to the cruel one’) resumes the word the heroine resisted in 1236, which Mu. Varadarasanar softens to ‘the one who is called cruel’. Pope: ‘My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain, / If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain?’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text, including the sandhi form வாடுதோட் பூசல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, unable to reach his wife, asks a passing rain-cloud to carry his message to her across India and tell her of his suffering and enduring love.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s poem makes an improvised messenger carry a separated lover’s complaint to the beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also searches for a go-between and settles on her own heart to carry her complaint.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s premise; strong on sending a lover’s complaint by an unusual messenger, though the sender is the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song begs others to carry word of her love-sickness to her absent beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sends her own heart on the same errand: to tell him how she wastes away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); near match on sending news of love-sickness to the beloved, though the messengers are other women, not her heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob refuses to air his grief before people and takes his complaint only to God.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s complaint likewise has one proper recipient: she would carry it only to the one who can end it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); parallel in directing a complaint to the one who can answer it, though Jacob’s recipient is God, not a lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I pour out my complaint before Him, I declare before Him my trouble.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist, alone in a cave, sets out his distress before the one who can help.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wants her heart to pour out the ‘clamour’ of her wasting body before her husband in the same way.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (142:2 in Christian numbering); good on declaring one’s trouble to the one who can help, but addressed to God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his long verses in the Theragatha, the monk Talaputa speaks directly to his own mind, reasoning with it, pleading with it and reproaching it, asking when it will at last do what he wishes.
buddhism.explanation: The Theragatha preserves a monk’s dramatic dialogue with his own heart.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns and addresses her heart as a separate person who could act for her.
buddhism.source: Theragatha 19, Talaputa (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a real parallel to apostrophising one’s own heart, but Talaputa urges his mind toward renunciation, not toward a lover.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines one form of arta-dhyana, ‘sorrowful brooding’, as the mind’s repeated dwelling on regaining a pleasing object from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology names exactly the anxious, circling thought that separation from the beloved produces, and classes it as karmically binding.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s urging of her heart to run to the absent one is such brooding, which Jain teaching would counsel her to still.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.31 (arta-dhyana on separation from the desired) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; precise on the mental state of longing in separation, but Jainism treats it as something to overcome rather than to voice.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Penelope opens her letter to Ulysses by telling him not to write back but to come himself, and then pours out the sleepless nights and fears she has endured while Troy has fallen and he still has not returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Heroides are letters in which waiting women send their complaints to absent men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has no letter, so she would send her heart to carry the complaint of her wasting body.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the letter’s opening and theme; strong fit on a wife sending her complaint to an absent husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius repeatedly speaks to his own soul as to another person, chiding it that it is doing itself wrong and that time to honour itself is running short.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor’s private notebook uses self-address to argue with his own mind.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also speaks to her heart as a separate agent, though to spur it toward love, not toward Stoic self-command.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.6 (paraphrase; cf. tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Next-best match; shares the form of addressing one’s own soul but not the content.

kurals.tamil:
முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது
பைந்தொடிப் பேதை நுதல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muyangiya kaikalai ookkap pasandhadhu
paindhotip paedhai nudhal.
kurals.meaning: The husband remembers: once, when I merely loosened my arms from our embrace, the forehead of my innocent girl with her golden bangles turned pale at once.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a little child holding a parent’s hand at a busy fair. If the parent lets go for just a second, the child’s face might look worried right away. The husband in this verse remembers that his wife looked worried and pale even when he let go of a hug for just a moment, so he knows how much she must be missing him now that he is far away.
kurals.university: With 1238 the voice changes: Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar gloss in the husband’s first person (‘when I loosened my arms’), and the traditional reading has the talaivaṉ, away from home, recalling his wife’s fragility to explain why he must hurry back. Muyaṅkiya kaikaḷai ūkka is ‘when [I] loosened (ūkka, ‘to slacken, withdraw’) the arms that embraced’; pacantatu… nutal, ‘the forehead turned sallow’, applies pacappu, the pallor of love-longing, to her brow, the classic site of a woman’s brightness (oḷ nutal, 1240). Paintoṭip pētai, ‘the innocent one with fresh-gold bangles’, uses pētai, ‘young, guileless woman’, a tender term. The logic is a fortiori: if a moment’s slackening paled her, what must long absence do? Solomon Pappaiah adds that he loosened his grip fearing his tight hold would hurt her. Pope: ‘One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked, / Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Bhavabhuti’s Uttararamacharita, Rama, looking at paintings of their forest exile, recalls how Sita used to fall asleep with her head on his arm, and his tenderness for her is mixed with the pain of knowing he must soon part from her.
hinduism.explanation: Bhavabhuti dwells on a husband’s memory of his wife’s closeness in his arms.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband likewise remembers the embrace and how fragile she was within it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the play, not verified this session; good on a husband’s tender recollection, but there is no detail of her paling when he loosens his hold.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song describes the beloved’s embrace as her rest and security.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse side of the same embrace: when it is loosened even slightly, the beloved’s brightness falters.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); same embrace image, though the Song celebrates it rather than its loosening.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes spouses as each other’s garment, close, protecting and covering.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows how a wife feels when that ‘garment’ is drawn back even for a moment.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); captures marital closeness, but nothing of distress at a moment’s separation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house.”
judaism.explanation: Having found her beloved after a night of searching, the woman of the Song will not loosen her hold.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, cannot bear even a slackened embrace; she pales the moment it loosens.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; strong on refusing to let go of the beloved, told from the woman’s side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From affection springs grief, from affection springs fear. For one who is wholly free from affection there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces grief and fear to affection itself.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s instant pallor at a loosened embrace is the fear that affection brings, exactly as the verse diagnoses.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; explains the feeling, but as something to be outgrown rather than cherished.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana’s lecture on carelessness teaches that one passionately attached to pleasant touch suffers as soon as it is withdrawn, and never finds satisfaction in it.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching treats attachment to touch as one of the senses’ bonds that produce pain at every loss.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s pallor at a slackened embrace is the pain of withdrawn touch; Jain doctrine would read it as the fruit of attachment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32, verses on touch (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; it reinterprets the Kural’s tenderness as attachment rather than echoing it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes what happens to her in the beloved’s presence: her tongue breaks, a fine fire runs under her skin, her ears hum, a sweat comes over her, and she is ‘greener than grass’, seeming to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: The most famous Greek poem of love-sickness names a greenish pallor as love’s mark on the body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pacappu, the sallow-green pallor that spreads over the wife’s forehead, is the same colour of love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; striking match on the green-sallow colour of love-sickness, though Sappho pales in the beloved’s presence, not at a parting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were split in two, so that each half longs for its other; when they find each other they embrace and do not want to be parted even for a moment.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth explains lovers’ desire never to loosen their embrace as a longing to be whole again.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife pales at a slackened embrace because, in Aristophanes’ terms, she feels herself made half again.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-192e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; strong on the unbearable smallest separation of lovers.

kurals.tamil:
முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழப் பசப்புற்ற
பேதை பெருமழைக் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muyakkidaith thanvali poazhap pasapputra
paedhai perumazhaik kan.
kurals.meaning: When even a breath of cool breeze slipped in between us as we embraced, the large, rain-cool eyes of my innocent girl turned pale.
kurals.elementary: Think of two friends sitting so close on a cold night that not even the wind can get between them. If a tiny gust slips in, one of them shivers. The husband here remembers that even a little breeze between them made his wife look sad, so he knows a long trip away must be very hard for her.
kurals.university: The husband’s recollection continues and intensifies 1238: now not his arms but a cool breeze (taṇ vaḷi) ‘split’ (pōḻa, ‘to cleave, pierce’) their embrace (muyakku iṭai, ‘in the midst of the embrace’), and at that hair’s-breadth separation her eyes, not her forehead, were touched with pacappu. Perumaḻaik kaṇ, ‘large rain-eyes’, is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘large eyes like rain’ (cool and moist) and by Kalaignar as ‘wide, long eyes’; the image may suggest both their coolness and their readiness for tears. Solomon Pappaiah ends his gloss with the husband’s worried question, ‘how must they be now?’, which captures the a fortiori logic of 1238-1240. Pope: ‘As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there; / The maid’s large liquid eyes were dimmed with care.’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, when Krishna suddenly vanishes from the circle of dancing gopis at night, they are overwhelmed at once, searching for him from tree to tree and asking the creepers and deer where he has gone.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows a moment’s disappearance of the beloved producing instant, overwhelming distress.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, is stricken by the smallest break in closeness, a breeze slipping between them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong on a brief separation causing deep distress, though the gopis’ love is read devotionally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher observes plainly that two together keep each other warm, and one alone cannot.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s cold breeze slipping between the lovers is exactly the chill the verse describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); neat match on closeness and cold, though the verse is practical wisdom rather than love poetry.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents spouses as a source of tranquillity for each other, bound by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows how fragile that tranquillity feels to a loving wife, broken even by a breath of air between them.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); about marital closeness in general, not distress at a slight separation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: A Talmudic proverb measures love by how little space a couple needs between them.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural the lovers’ closeness is so complete that even a breeze in the gap is felt as a wound.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; vivid match on love measured by the space between bodies, though the proverb is used to illustrate God and Israel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Canda-Kinnara Jataka, a pair of kinnaras are separated for a single night when a sudden flood fills the stream between them; they spend the night calling to each other, and for the rest of their long lives they grieve over that one lost night.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka makes a single night’s separation the cause of lifelong lament between devoted mates.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife reacts the same way to the slightest gap, a breeze in the embrace.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka 485) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Jataka from general knowledge, not verified this session; strong match on a tiny separation magnified by love.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Pavananjaya, encamped on a campaign, sees a female chakravaka bird crying all night for her mate, from whom she is parted till dawn; realising that his neglected wife Anjana must suffer far more, he secretly flies back to her that very night.
jainism.explanation: The Jain narrative makes a bird’s single night of separation open a husband’s eyes to his wife’s pain.
jainism.tie_back: Like Pavananjaya, the Kural’s husband reasons from a small separation, a breeze in an embrace, to how much his wife must suffer in a long absence.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain story (also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya), not verified against Johnson’s text this session; strong on the husband’s a fortiori reasoning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Ceyx resolves to sail to consult an oracle, his wife Alcyone turns pale, weeps and begs him not to go, or at least to take her with him, since even a short parting by sea terrifies her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s devoted wife cannot bear the thought of even a brief separation from her husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife pales at a breath of wind between them; Alcyone pales at the mere mention of a voyage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on a wife’s pallor at separation, though Alcyone fears a real danger rather than reacting to a breeze.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says lovers clasp and press each other close, mouth to mouth, yet can take nothing from each other, since body cannot pass into body, and so even the tightest embrace leaves a gap that desire cannot close.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet sees in lovers’ embraces a longing for a total union that bodies cannot achieve.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s breeze slipping into the embrace is the gap Lucretius points to, felt by the wife as a wound.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1105-1111 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the gap that remains in an embrace, though Lucretius uses it to criticise passion.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே
ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannin pasappoa paruvaral eydhindrae
onnudhal seydhadhu kandu.
kurals.meaning: Was it from seeing what her bright forehead had done, turning pale, that the pallor in her eyes itself became so sorrowful?
kurals.elementary: When one person in a family is sad, the others often feel sad too, just from seeing them. In this verse the husband imagines his wife’s face as a little family: when her forehead turned pale, her eyes saw it and became even sadder.
kurals.university: The closing couplet is a conceit (taṟkuṟippēṟṟa aṇi, poetic fancy) in which parts of the wife’s face react to one another. Kaṇṇiṉ pacappō paruvaral eytiṉṟē, ‘did the pallor of the eyes fall into distress?’, uses the particle ō for wondering doubt, and oṇ nutal ceytatu kaṇṭu, ‘having seen what the bright forehead did’, refers back to 1238, where the forehead paled first. Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar read: seeing the forehead turn sallow, the pallor of her eyes grew into greater suffering. Solomon Pappaiah offers a different reading, in which the eye, once ashamed before the forehead’s delicacy, now shares its distress. The chapter thus ends where it began, with the eyes (1231), now joined by the forehead, so that the ‘wasting of the limbs’ is complete from head to arm. Pope: ‘The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now, / Beholding what was done by that bright brow.’ Text identical on both sites; ytamizh’s transliteration renders the archaic eytiṉṟē as ‘eydhindrae’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Chandogya Upanishad, the senses and breath quarrel over which is greatest; each departs for a year and the body carries on, but when breath begins to leave, all the others are torn loose with it and beg it to stay.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad pictures the body’s faculties as a community that rises or falls together.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s eye grieving at the forehead’s pallor is a small, tender version of the same solidarity of the body’s parts.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; shares the interdependence of bodily parts, but its subject is the primacy of breath, not love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the community as a body whose parts feel each other’s pain.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural pictures this literally: when the forehead suffers, the eyes suffer with it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close match on parts of a body sharing each other’s suffering, though Paul’s body is the church.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a loving community to a body whose parts share each other’s illness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes share the forehead’s ‘illness’ of pallor in just this way.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong on the body’s parts sharing suffering, though the subject is the community of believers.

judaism.quote_or_event: Isaiah pictures a people so afflicted that the whole head is sick and the whole heart faint, with no soundness from the sole of the foot to the head.
judaism.explanation: The prophet describes suffering that spreads through every part of the body.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wasting likewise spreads from part to part, until even the eyes grieve at the forehead’s pallor.
judaism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase (not re-verified this session); shares spreading bodily affliction, but as rebuke, not sympathy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha summarises dependent arising: when this is, that is; from the arising of this comes the arising of that.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching sees every state as conditioned by others, arising together.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ grief arising from the forehead’s pallor is a poetic picture of one condition giving rise to another.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 79, Culasakuludayi Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as paraphrase; the conditioning principle fits the conceit, but the sutta is metaphysical and has nothing to do with love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra states that the function of souls is to render service to one another (parasparopagraho jivanam).
jainism.explanation: This aphorism, now the motto of the Jain community, teaches that living beings exist in mutual support.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes grieving with the forehead are a tender picture of mutual support between parts that share one life.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra; good on mutual sympathy, though it speaks of souls, not parts of one body.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Narcissus wastes away at the pool, Echo, though still hurt by his rejection, grieves to see him; each time he cries ‘alas’, she echoes ‘alas’, and when he says ‘farewell’ she says ‘farewell’ too.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo shares in the wasting of the one she loves, repeating his grief back to him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise mirror and deepen the grief they see in the forehead.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on one suffering being sorrowing at another’s wasting, though Echo and Narcissus are two persons, not two features of one face.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that the best-ordered city is most like a single person: when a finger is hurt, the whole community of body and soul feels it and suffers together with the injured part.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the body’s shared feeling of pain as the model for social unity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural pictures the same shared feeling within one face: the eyes suffer with the pale forehead.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic 462c-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; close on parts of a body sharing pain, though Plato’s purpose is political.
